question.:question/problem:
Susan, the new receptionist of the Smithsonian Museum in Washington DC, uses the following three functions to model the daily number of visitors to the museum $t$ minutes after the museum has opened.

- $N(t)$ - the number of people inside the museum
- $E(t)$ - the rate at which people enter the museum
- $L(t)$ - the rate at which people leave the museum

What is the relationship between the three functions above?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The function $N(t)$ gives the number of people inside the museum $t$ minutes after opening. Then,

$$
N'(t) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}N(t)}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\textrm{Change in }N}{\textrm{Change in }t}.
$$

Thus, $N'(t)$ gives the rate at which the number of people inside the museum changes $t$ minutes after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of people inside the museum at time $t$ by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time $t.$ That is,

$$
N'(t) = E(t) - L(t).
$$

The change ratio denotes an instantaneous rate: the limit of change ratios as the time interval tends to zero.

Susan, the new receptionist of the Smithsonian Museum in Washington DC, uses the following three functions to model the daily number of visitors to the museum $u$ minutes after the museum has opened.

- $A(u)$ - the number of people inside the museum
- $S(u)$ - the rate at which people enter the museum
- $E(u)$ - the rate at which people leave the museum

What is the relationship between the three functions above?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The function $A(u)$ gives the number of people inside the museum $u$ minutes after opening. Then,

$$
A'(u) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}A(u)}{\textrm{d}u} = \dfrac{\textrm{Change in }A}{\textrm{Change in }u}.
$$

Thus, $A'(u)$ gives the rate at which the number of people inside the museum changes $u$ minutes after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of people inside the museum at time $u$ by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time $u.$ That is,

$$
A'(u) = S(u) - E(u).
$$

The change ratio denotes an instantaneous rate: the limit of change ratios as the time interval tends to zero.

question.:question/problem:
Jason, a biologist, is measuring the growth of bacteria in a Petri dish by recording the following two numbers for different values of $u,$ where $u$ is the time, in hours, since he started his observations:

- $P(u)$ - the number of bacteria in the dish.

- $q(u)$ - the rate at which the number of bacteria in the dish is increasing.

What is the relationship between $P(u)$ and $q(u)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The function $P(u)$ gives the number of bacteria inside the dish after $u$ hours. Then,

$$
{P}^{′}(u)=\frac{\text{d}P(u)}{\text{d}u}=\frac{\text{Change in }P}{\text{Change in }u}.
$$

Thus, ${P}^{′}(u)$ gives the rate at which the number of bacteria is increasing at time $u$, which is the same as $q(u).$ Therefore, the relationship between $P(u)$ and $q(u)$ is ${P}^{′}(u)=q(u).$

The change ratio denotes an instantaneous rate: the limit of change ratios as the time interval tends to zero.

Jason, a biologist, is measuring the growth of bacteria in a Petri dish by recording the following two numbers for different values of $u,$ where $u$ is the time, in hours, since he started his observations:

- $O(u)$ - the number of bacteria in the dish.

- $s(u)$ - the rate at which the number of bacteria in the dish is increasing.

What is the relationship between $O(u)$ and $s(u)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The function $O(u)$ gives the number of bacteria inside the dish after $u$ hours. Then,

$$
{O}^{′}(u)=\frac{\text{d}O(u)}{\text{d}u}=\frac{\text{Change in }O}{\text{Change in }u}.
$$

Thus, ${O}^{′}(u)$ gives the rate at which the number of bacteria is increasing at time $u$, which is the same as $s(u).$ Therefore, the relationship between $O(u)$ and $s(u)$ is ${O}^{′}(u)=s(u).$

The change ratio denotes an instantaneous rate: the limit of change ratios as the time interval tends to zero.

The function $P(u)$ gives the number of children inside the playground $u$ hours after opening. Then,

$$
{P}^{′}(u)=\frac{\text{d}P(u)}{\text{d}u}=\frac{\text{Change in }P}{\text{Change in }u}.
$$

Thus, ${P}^{′}(u)$ gives the rate at which the number of children inside the playground changes $u$ hours after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of children inside the playground at time $u$ by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time $u.$ That is,

$$
{P}^{′}(u)=Q(u)-B(u).
$$

The change ratio denotes an instantaneous rate: the limit of change ratios as the time interval tends to zero.

- $B(u)$ - the number of children inside the playground

- $C(u)$ - the rate at which children enter the playground

- $W(u)$ - the rate at which children leave the playground

What is the relationship between the functions above?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The function $B(u)$ gives the number of children inside the playground $u$ hours after opening. Then,

$$
{B}^{′}(u)=\frac{\text{d}B(u)}{\text{d}u}=\frac{\text{Change in }B}{\text{Change in }u}.
$$

Thus, ${B}^{′}(u)$ gives the rate at which the number of children inside the playground changes $u$ hours after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of children inside the playground at time $u$ by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time $u.$ That is,

$$
{B}^{′}(u)=C(u)-W(u).
$$

The change ratio denotes an instantaneous rate: the limit of change ratios as the time interval tends to zero.

To measure the number of children visiting a playground, Noah uses the following three functions that model the hourly number of visitors to the playground $u$ hours after the playground is opened to the public.

- $P(u)$ - the number of children inside the playground

- $A(u)$ - the rate at which children enter the playground

- $H(u)$ - the rate at which children leave the playground

What is the relationship between the functions above?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The function $P(u)$ gives the number of children inside the playground $u$ hours after opening. Then,

$$
{P}^{′}(u)=\frac{\text{d}P(u)}{\text{d}u}=\frac{\text{Change in }P}{\text{Change in }u}.
$$

Thus, ${P}^{′}(u)$ gives the rate at which the number of children inside the playground changes $u$ hours after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of children inside the playground at time $u$ by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time $u.$ That is,

$$
{P}^{′}(u)=A(u)-H(u).
$$

The change ratio denotes an instantaneous rate: the limit of change ratios as the time interval tends to zero.

Douglas, a pilot, is flying a plane. The plane's control systems record two measurements for different values of $s,$ where $s$ is the time, in minutes, since take off. The two measurements are:

- $B(s)$ - the altitude (height) of the plane

- $u(s)$ the rate at which the altitude is increasing

What is the relationship between $B(s)$ and $u(s)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The function $B(s)$ gives the altitude of the plane after $s$ minutes. Then,

$$
{B}^{′}(s)=\frac{\text{d}B(s)}{\text{d}s}=\frac{\text{Change in }B}{\text{Change in }s}.
$$

Thus, ${B}^{′}(s)$ gives the rate at which the altitude is increasing at time $s$, which is the same as $u(s).$ Therefore, the relationship between $B(s)$ and $u(s)$ is ${B}^{′}(s)=u(s).$

The change ratio denotes an instantaneous rate: the limit of change ratios as the time interval tends to zero.

- $P(u)$ - the number of items in a store, in items.

$$
P'(u)=\frac{\text{d}P(u)}{\text{d}u}=\frac{\text{Change in }P}{\text{Change in }u}.

Thus, $P'(u)$ gives the instantaneous rate of change of that amount. This is the same as $q(u)$. Therefore, the relationship is $P'(u)=q(u)$.
